common_name: Auburn Crimson Clover (Classic Early Reseeding Southern Cover Crop Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in early fall so plants establish before hard frost; Auburn matures at roughly the same pace as Dixie, ahead of later reseeding types like Chief, Kentucky Pride, and Talladega.

directions: Auburn is one of the earliest reseeding crimson clover cultivars developed in the mid-twentieth century South, released alongside Dixie as part of a USDA and land-grant breeding effort that gave crimson clover the ability to volunteer itself from hard seed rather than needing annual replanting. It fixes substantial nitrogen through fall and winter growth before producing the classic elongated crimson flower spikes in spring, which are heavily worked by early-season bees ahead of seed set. Broadcast or drill seed onto a firm, weed-free fall seedbed for the strongest stand, and either terminate at early bloom for maximum nitrogen release or let a portion mature to maintain a self-sustaining planting. Though largely superseded in modern trials by later Auburn University and Mississippi State releases such as AU Robin, Tibbee, and Talladega, it remains historically important as one of the founding named crimson clover selections.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Materials Program
Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Bowie Buffalograss (Early Improved Seeded Turf Cultivar)

planting.note: Direct sow into warm soil after the last frost and keep the surface consistently moist through the two- to three-week germination period.

directions: Bowie is an early improved seeded buffalograss selection from the University of Nebraska turfgrass breeding program, part of the same lineage that produced Cody, Sundancer, and the vegetative cultivars 609, Density, and Legacy. It offered a step up in density and color over the older seeded standard Texoka when it was released, though later, faster-establishing seeded cultivars have since become the more common recommendation. Once established it shares the species' hallmark extreme drought tolerance and minimal fertility needs, forming a low, fine-leaved sod that persists through Great Plains winters with little input. Mow high and infrequently at 3 to 5 inches, or leave unmowed for a relaxed, low-water native lawn.

planting.note: Sow into warm, well-prepared soil once temperatures hold reliably above 65°F and keep evenly moist until germination is complete.

directions: Prestige is a seeded buffalograss cultivar from the University of Nebraska and Native Turf Group breeding program, developed for better density and turf quality than older seeded selections like Texoka, in the same generation of releases that produced Sundancer. It establishes from seed sown into warm soil rather than from plugs or sod, making it more economical to cover large areas even though it fills in more slowly than vegetatively propagated cultivars. Like other buffalograss selections it needs very little supplemental water or nitrogen once rooted in, going dormant and straw-colored through winter and greening back reliably each spring. Mow occasionally at 3 to 4 inches for a tidier lawn, or leave unmowed for a naturalized, prairie-style planting.

common_name: Remonta Oilseed Radish (European Biofumigant Cover Crop Radish)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill 6 to 10 weeks before the first fall frost into a firm, well-prepared seedbed.

directions: Remonta is a German-bred European oilseed radish cultivar imported for North American cover crop use alongside sibling selections such as Colonel and Adagio, and it has performed comparably to those cultivars for total dry-matter production in Midwest field trials. It germinates within days of sowing and quickly builds a broad leaf rosette over a shorter, more branched taproot than a daikon-type tillage radish, scavenging residual soil nitrogen before winter leaching losses. Like other high-glucosinolate oilseed radish types, its tissue offers some biofumigant suppression of soilborne pathogens as the residue breaks down after a hard freeze. In most winters north of the Gulf South it winterkills cleanly, leaving an easily worked, nutrient-rich mulch ahead of spring planting.
sources: Michigan State University Extension — Bulletin E2907

planting.note: Sow fresh seed on the surface in fall, or divide established clumps, in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade to part shade.

directions: Flore Pleno is a double-flowered heirloom selection of greater celandine, replacing the wild species' simple four-petaled blooms with small, pompom-like clusters of golden-yellow petals held above the same lobed, blue-gray foliage. Because the doubled flowers set little to no viable seed, this cultivar spreads far more slowly than the free-seeding wild type, making it a better-behaved choice for cottage and woodland borders. Grow it in the same dry shade and disturbed soil the species tolerates, dividing congested clumps in fall to increase stock. Handle broken stems with care, since the bright orange latex sap is caustic and can irritate skin, exactly as in the straight species.

common_name: Fair Ellen Oak-Leaf Geranium (Deep-Cut Scented Pelargonium)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; overwinter indoors outside zones 9-11.

directions: Fair Ellen is a selection of oak-leaf geranium prized for foliage cut even more deeply and finely than the species, giving the sticky, aromatic leaves a lacy, almost fern-like outline while keeping the same pungent bitter-almond to balsamic fragrance when brushed. It grows into a noticeably more compact, denser shrub than seedling oak-leaf geranium, making it easier to manage in pots and mixed scented-herb plantings. Root stem cuttings in a lean, fast-draining mix and grow in full sun with light, infrequent watering, since rich soil or excess moisture produces soft, less fragrant growth. It has no cold tolerance and must be overwintered as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen outside the warmest zones.
sources: Herb Society of America — scented geraniums guide

common_name: Pusillus Dwarf Sweet Flag (Miniature Japanese Sweet Flag)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil or shallow water in shade to part shade.

directions: Pusillus is an extremely diminutive, solid-green cultivar of Japanese sweet flag, forming dense tufts of fine, grass-like leaves only two to three inches tall — among the smallest named selections of the species in cultivation. Its miniature scale suits container water gardens, trough plantings, bonsai underplanting, and other small-scale settings better than open pond margins, where larger cultivars like 'Ogon' or 'Variegatus' are more typical. Divide congested clumps in spring and replant in humus-rich, consistently moist soil or shallow standing water in shade to part shade. Unlike its gold- and white-variegated relatives, Pusillus is grown purely for its tiny scale and fine texture rather than leaf color.
